name: Walton Belt Vibrator

lead: The Walton belt vibrator belongs to the family of vibrating belt machines: a motor on a post vibrates a wide fabric belt held around the waist or hips. Marketing promoted it as a way to reduce fat and slim the figure without exercise.
The appeal was a slimmer midsection with no effort. Reports describe such machines as fading from fashion by the 1980s once fat reduction was not borne out.

paras: The user stood on a platform and leaned against one or two belts attached to a motor so the belt vibrated the targeted area, such as the abdomen or hips.
Vibration machines of this type are described as ineffective for fat loss; general cautions for mechanical vibration apply to people with medical conditions.

angle.text: Advertising presented the belt as a way to reduce abdominal fat passively. It also served as a massage-style relaxation device.

lead: Vibrating belt machines were marketed as a passive way to slim the body. A Walton Manufacturing Company Mark II belt vibrator, circa 1960, from Dallas, Texas, is held in a museum collection.

The user stood at a platform with a waist-high post holding a motor, leaned away, and let a belt vibrate the area to be reduced, especially the abdomen [1]. Early versions by Gustav Zander in the late 1800s were intended as massage [1].

paras: A platform with a post rising to waist level holds an electric motor with one or two wide fabric belts attached [1].

John Harvey Kellogg promoted a version as the Battle Creek Health Builder from 1927, and an actress appeared in a November 1927 Vogue advertisement [1]. Fat-reduction marketing was widespread in the 1950s and 1960s and the machines faded by the 1980s; they became a comic staple on television in I Love Lucy and The Flintstones [1].
